transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Riley (Redwood), Marco (NovaScale), Samantha (NovaScale), Anand (NovaScale), Dina (NovaScale)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial): Hybrid quantization caused small but reproducible accuracy drop (~1.5-3% on internal eval A). Customer sees larger drift on certain prompt families. Action: share quant profiles, run on-prem microbenchmarks, start bisect.

00:00 Ethan: Okay, hey everyone thanks for joining, let's do a quick rund— round of intros, and then we'll jump into the regression details and the on‑prem plan.
00:22 Marco: Hey, Marco here, lead ML, quick context: we rolled INT8+AWQ across our LLMs last week and saw throughput improvements but also a visible drop in metric on our classification tasks, like precision down about, uh, 2-ish percent.
00:38 Priya: Thanks Marco. Just to confirm, you used the hybrid profile we shared last month or you used the aggressive AWQ packing?
00:45 Marco: It's the hybrid— we used the hybrid profile but we flipped the AWQ block-mode on for the second pass. Not sure if that part got lost.
00:54 Riley: (mumbles) got it. So examples of prompts where you see the drift — are they long context or short?
01:05 Marco: Mostly long context, 1k+ tokens where we also rely heavily on KV cache to avoid re-compute.
01:12 Samantha: And on the infra side, we're on-prem, 8x A100 80GB, Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.1, cuDNN 9.3, custom driver 535 — we wanted to make sure this environment was in scope.
01:28 Ethan: Great, that helps. Two immediate suspects: quantization scheme interacting with KV cache eviction/restore, and some fused kernels in AWQ/GPTQ that differ across cuda/cuDNN versions.
01:42 Dina: From security, we also want to ensure the artifacts we share don't include customer data and that we use KMS-protected bundles for any logs.
01:50 Priya: Absolutely, we'll scrub prompts; we'll provide synthetic eval slices and config files.
02:05 Marco: Quick note, we also tried a FP8 experiment with the same model and that had smaller accuracy impact but worse memory pressure.
02:15 Riley: Yeah FP8 is promising but it depends a lot on headcount — I mean per-layer sensitivity. Some attention heads blow up with naive FP8.
02:26 Priya: Right — which is why the hybrid approach tries to keep critical layers in FP16/FP32 and quantize others. Our hybrid profile keeps first n layers in FP16 and uses AWQ for the rest.
02:38 Anand: Is there a canonical way you recommend we measure the regression? Our internal eval has multiple families — classification, summarization, QA — which should we prioritize?
02:50 Priya: Start with the family that regressed the most — you said classification — we'll provide an eval subset A that mirrors that workload. Also run per-prompt perplexity and a token-level diff script we can share.
03:05 Marco: Cool. For the KV cache, we noticed that on long contexts the generated tokens sometimes degrade after a cache restore — like the model's next-token distributions shift. Could that be a precision/rounding artifact?
03:20 Riley: Possible. If the KV cache is stored in quantized form or if there's a conversion step during restore, small numeric differences can amplify down the stack. Also batching-induced reordering can surface differences.
03:36 Priya: We should check whether you're using prefix-cache or a streaming restore; prefix/KV cache modes differ in how they serialize dtypes.
03:46 Samantha: We're using a custom streaming restore — it's optimized to send only changed chunks. Might be doing an extra cast. We'll capture the end-to-end trace.
03:57 Ethan: Yeah, please capture the exact buffer dtype on save/restore, and the step where you do the dequant path.
04:05 Marco: One more thing — we saw the regression more pronounced when client-side batching increased (batches of 8+). With batch size 1 the drop is smaller.
04:16 Priya: That aligns with a batching schedule mismatch — if you batch across request lengths and the runtime uses a different kernel path for batched tokens, quant rounding behavior can differ. We'll look at continuous batching heuristics.
04:30 Riley: Also checking kernel selection: some fused attention kernels operate in FP32 accumulation vs FP16 depending on kernel/compute capability — that affects final numeric results.
04:42 Marco: Can you explain the difference between GPTQ and AWQ in terms of numeric stability?
04:50 Priya: Briefly: GPTQ is per-channel quant optimized for transformer weights, tends to be stable but larger per-layer error; AWQ (A-weighted Q) focuses on activation-weight matching and often yields better throughput but sometimes worse corner-case accuracy. Implementation details vary and small differences in reorder/fusing can change results.
05:12 Dina: From compliance — if we need to run Redwood's code on-prem, what's the licensing and review process?
05:20 Ethan: We'll send the bill of materials and EULA; for on-prem test harness we can provide a vetted binary and source snapshot under NDA.
05:30 Samantha: OK. Let's focus the triage: what experiments do we run first?
05:36 Riley: First experiment: reproducibility on a single node with identical seed using FP16 baseline, INT8 (GPTQ), AWQ hybrid, and FP8. Collect logits, per-token probs, and output diffs on eval subset.
05:50 Priya: Second experiment: KV cache serialization test — save/restore after N tokens and compare logits. Third: batching matrix — vary batch sizes and seq lengths.
06:02 Marco: Sounds good. Are there any known hot kernels we should avoid? We saw a kernel crash once when using awq block size 64.
06:12 Priya: We'll include recommended safe kernel flags; AWQ block sizes of 32 or 16 are generally more stable on A100 for certain driver versions, but that also affects speed. We'll include perf tradeoffs.
06:26 Anand: About drivers — could driver versions explain the delta between Redwood-hosted benchmarks and our private infra?
06:33 Riley: Absolutely. cuBLAS/cuDNN optimizations, kernel launch behaviors, and math library implementations vary across drivers and CUDA versions; small numerical shifts can cascade. We'll provide a matrix of recommended driver/cuda combinations.
06:47 Marco: For the bisect, will you provide scripts to flip per-layer quant thresholds?
06:52 Riley: Yes — small python harness that can re-quantize layer n with FP16 while others are quantized, to isolate which layer causes most regression. We'll open source the harness under the engagement NDA.
07:05 Priya: We'll also share a lightweight tooling to capture runtime traces (kernel selection, dtype casts, batching decisions) without shipping PII.
07:18 Samantha: On the infra side, we can afford to run both the microbench and a 24-hour soak run if needed. We'll schedule per your timelines.
07:30 Ethan: Good. Quick question on fallback policy: would you prefer automatic fallback to FP16 on regression signals, or a canary rollout?
07:40 Marco: Canary rollout first, auto-fallback only with strong guards. We want visibility.
07:47 Priya: Makes sense. We'll provide a rollout plan: canary to 5% traffic, monitor eval traces, then increase.
07:57 Dina: We'll need audit logs for any automatic fallbacks— retention and RBAC requirements.
08:05 Ethan: We'll include the console and audit hooks in the proposal.
08:12 Marco: Anything else on batching/KV interactions?
08:18 Riley: One more note: prefix caching with quantized KVs can be numerically stable if you store in FP16 locally and compress for transfer; storing quantized KVs to reduce transfer can introduce rounding artifacts.
08:34 Samantha: Interesting — currently we compress to reduce network; maybe we should try storing FP16 locally and only compress on transfer.
08:42 Marco: We'll run that variant.
08:48 Priya: Great. Also, for FP8 tests, watch out for head overflow — we'll include guardrails and a per-layer overflow metric.
09:00 Ethan: Alright let's recap and assign owners. Action items we'll follow up in an email with links: quant profiles, bisect script, eval subset, and the recommended driver matrix.
09:15 Marco: Quick question — any known regressions that reverted when switching quant rounding mode from nearest to stochastic?
09:24 Riley: In some experiments stochastic rounding helped on classification but hurt generation coherence. It's a tradeoff; we'll include both variants in the test matrix.
09:38 Priya: We'll also run a token-diff smoke test to see if the model diverges quickly after the cache restore point; that will help pinpoint where the numeric drift starts.
09:50 Samantha: We'll capture perf counters and kernel selection logs (nsight-like) and share them.
10:00 Ethan: Perfect. We'll aim to get the initial artifacts to you by Friday 2025-07-11.
10:07 Marco: Thanks everyone, appreciate it.
